body: {"total":5,"records":[{"title":"Clinically indicated versus routine replacement of peripheral intravenous catheters after a policy change: a before-after cohort on four surgical wards","authors":"Adebayo-Lindqvist T, Moreau-Kaplan S, Hughes-Oyelowo R","year":2017,"venue":"Northfold Vascular Access Nursing","doi":"10.5555/nvan.2017.0215","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Four surgical wards changed from routine replacement of peripheral intravenous catheters every 72 hours to replacement only when clinically indicated. We compared 2,310 catheters inserted in the six months before the change with 2,188 catheters inserted in the six months after. Catheter failure, defined as removal for phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion or dislodgement before the end of treatment, occurred in 31 percent of catheters before and 33 percent after. Median dwell time rose from 58 to 81 hours, and the number of catheters inserted per 100 patient-days fell from 36 to 27. Phlebitis was recorded for 6 percent of catheters in both periods. The comparison used ward records without adjustment for patient mix or for other changes on the wards."},{"title":"Monthly catheter failure before and after a switch to clinically indicated replacement: an interrupted time series in a general hospital","authors":"Grey-Olawale M, Fenwick-Duarte S","year":2015,"venue":"Hospital Nursing Quality Reports","doi":"10.5555/hnqr.2015.0093","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A general hospital switched all adult wards from routine replacement of peripheral catheters every 72 hours to clinically indicated replacement. We plotted the monthly proportion of catheters removed for failure for 18 months before and 18 months after the switch and fitted a segmented regression. Failure was 28 percent in the month before the switch, and there was no step change at the switch (0.9 percentage points, 95 percent confidence interval -2.1 to 3.9) and no change in slope. A change of catheter brand eight months after the switch coincided with a short rise in occlusions. The analysis used ward-level monthly counts and could not account for patients with several catheters."},{"title":"Shift-by-shift phlebitis scoring and catheter dwell beyond 96 hours on medical wards: an observational study","authors":"Oyelaran-Castaneda B, Lindgren-Adu P, Whitcombe-Sato K","year":2022,"venue":"Tarnvale Infusion Practice","doi":"10.5555/tip.2022.0147","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"After the hospital adopted clinically indicated replacement, nurses on three medical wards scored insertion sites every shift with a five-point phlebitis scale. Of 1,694 catheters, 431 stayed in place beyond 96 hours. The rate of phlebitis did not rise with dwell beyond 96 hours: 4.1 per 1,000 catheter-days up to 96 hours and 3.8 per 1,000 catheter-days afterwards. Site assessment was documented in 83 percent of shifts, and documentation was least complete at night and at weekends. Catheters with incomplete site documentation were more often removed for infiltration. The study could not examine bloodstream infection because only two occurred."},{"title":"Routine resiting and the pain of repeated insertion in adult medical inpatients: a two-hospital cohort","authors":"Petrakis-Nwosu E, Salgado-Whitfield M","year":2020,"venue":"Clinical Nursing Evidence Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 406 adult medical inpatients with a peripheral intravenous catheter at two hospitals, one with a policy of routine resiting every 96 hours and one replacing catheters only when clinically indicated. Patients at the routine resiting hospital had a median of three insertions per admission, against two at the other hospital. Patients rated the pain of each observed insertion on a scale from 0 to 10; 38 percent of patients at the routine resiting hospital reported at least one insertion scored 7 or higher, against 24 percent at the other hospital. Catheter failure was similar at the two hospitals. Patient mix differed between the hospitals, and pain was recorded only for insertions that a research nurse observed."},{"title":"Infiltration with longer peripheral catheter dwell in inpatients aged 75 and over: an observational study on two medical wards","authors":"Solberg-Nakamura T, Achebe-Quist L","year":2025,"venue":"Gerontological Nursing Practice","doi":"10.5555/gnp.2025.0044","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 812 peripheral catheters in patients aged 75 and over on two medical wards that used clinically indicated replacement. Infiltration occurred in 14 percent of catheters and became more frequent after the fourth day of dwell (hazard ratio 1.6 for each further day, 95 percent confidence interval 1.2 to 2.1). Most infiltrations were found at the scheduled site check rather than reported by patients, and infiltrations in patients with delirium were found later than in other patients. Phlebitis was uncommon. The two wards had higher nurse staffing than the hospital average, which may limit how far the findings apply."}]}
